planting.note: Plant offsets or nursery starts in spring into fast-draining cactus mix in full sun; the sprawling, clustering stems benefit from a wide, shallow container or a raised bed.

directions: Native to the dry Chaco scrublands of Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, and Brazil, this clustering columnar cactus sends up slender, densely golden-spined stems that lean and sprawl rather than standing fully upright. In summer it produces curved, tubular, bright orange-red flowers that stay nearly closed and are pollinated by hummingbirds rather than opening wide for bees like most cactus blooms. Grow it in gritty, mineral cactus soil in full sun, watering only when the soil has dried completely, and protect it from temperatures below the high 20s°F. Older clumps form a dense mound of arching stems that work well massed in a xeriscape bed or raised container display.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated starts in spring into a raised, gravel-mulched scree or trough bed with extremely sharp drainage; never use wild-collected plants, as this species is federally protected.

directions: One of the smallest cacti in North America, Knowlton's cactus forms tight clusters of pea- to marble-sized stems barely rising above the gravelly soil of its extremely limited native range near the Colorado-New Mexico border, where it is a federally listed endangered species. In April it produces disproportionately large, pale pink flowers that nearly hide the tiny plant body. Specialty rock-garden and cactus nurseries propagate it from seed or division for collectors, and it should only ever be purchased as nursery-grown stock. Site it in a raised trough or scree bed with bone-dry winter dormancy and mineral grit rather than organic soil, since excess moisture around the crown is the most common cause of loss in cultivation.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service species profile

planting.note: Plant divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in a cool site with light shade and reliable snow cover or consistent moisture through winter.

directions: This mat-forming alpine heather carpets rocky, snow-fed slopes from Japan through the Aleutians and into the coastal mountains of the Pacific Northwest, its trailing stems densely clothed in tiny scale-like leaves that give it the look of a flattened clubmoss rather than a typical shrub. In late spring, slender white bell-shaped flowers dangle on short reddish stalks just above the foliage, one per shoot tip. It demands the cool, consistently moist, acidic conditions of a true alpine garden and resents hot, dry summers or standing water alike, making it best suited to a trough, scree bed, or peat-sand rock garden mix with light afternoon shade. Established mats are long-lived where summers stay cool, but struggle in lowland heat.

planting.note: Plant the tuber horizontally just under the substrate surface in a submerged aquarium or pond container in nutrient-rich, fine substrate; this species is grown fully underwater, not as a marginal or bog plant.

directions: Native to slow-moving rivers and streams in Madagascar, this submerged aquatic plant is prized for leaves reduced to a lattice of translucent veins with almost no solid leaf tissue between them, giving each blade the look of fine green lace. It is grown entirely underwater in aquariums or water gardens, rooted from a tuber in fine, nutrient-rich substrate with bright but indirect light and cool-to-moderate water temperatures, since it tends to go dormant and can rot in prolonged warm water above the mid-70s°F. Many growers lift and rest the tuber in damp sand for a few months each year to mimic its natural dry-season dormancy and keep it flourishing long term. Its delicate foliage is easily damaged by algae or heavy biofilm, so pairing it with shrimp or snails to keep the leaves clean is a common practice.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or nursery starts in spring into lean, sharply drained, gritty soil in full sun; this hybrid clone does not come true from seed.

directions: A deeper-colored sibling of the better-known 'Warley Rose', this compact Persian stonecress hybrid forms a tidy mound of small blue-gray leaves that disappears under a flush of richer, rosy-red four-petaled flowers in late spring. Like its relative, it thrives in lean, gritty, fast-draining soil and full sun, performing best where summers are hot and dry rather than humid, and it is prone to rotting out in rich or poorly drained ground. Being a hybrid clone, it must be propagated by softwood cuttings taken just after flowering rather than by seed, which will not reproduce the true flower color. Shear lightly after bloom to keep the mound tight and encourage fresh growth for next year's display.
